title: Bram and the Smile
premise: August Crane, a skeptical urban explorer, discovers a network of tunnels beneath her late grandmother's house that appear on no survey — and when every mirror in the house begins reflecting the room one second late, she is pulled through into 1974, where something wearing her grandmother's face is waiting. The entity, called the Smile, survives by trading faces: it took her grandmother's reflection and her memory of a stolen summer, and now it wants August's. To escape, August must return what was taken in 1974 — a drowned child's photograph hidden in the tunnel walls — before the lag between mirror and room stretches to a full minute and traps her permanently on the wrong side of the glass. In the end she gives the Smile not her face but her worst memory, freeing her grandmother's ghost and sealing the tunnels at the cost of forgetting why she ever went down.
about_author: Theo Kavanagh is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent a decade cataloguing unmapped spaces beneath Midwestern towns before turning to horror full-time. Their fiction draws on real architectural anomalies and the unsettling conviction that some rooms remember being built.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: POV August. August inherits her estranged grandmother's house and, unable to sleep in it, begins mapping its basement with LiDAR out of professional habit. The scan reveals a corridor behind the foundation wall that matches no blueprint. Emotional beat: restless curiosity masking grief she refuses to name.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: POV August. While brushing her teeth, August notices her bathroom mirror lags — her reflection blinks after she does. She tests it with a metronome app: exactly one second. Every mirror in the house agrees. Emotional beat: rational denial curdling into the first cold drop of fear.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept Down There
chapters.summary: POV August. Behind the foundation wall August finds a hand-dug tunnel lined with wallpaper from decades past, ending at a bricked arch scratched with tally marks — hundreds of them. A child's shoe sits in the dust. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery soured by evidence someone lived down here.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Won't Look Up
chapters.summary: POV August. Elderly neighbor Ruth Voss warns August off the house without explaining, then lets slip one detail: 'Your grandma came back wrong in '74.' August dismisses it, but photographs her grandmother's old albums and finds every picture from that summer face-bleached. Emotional beat: dread arriving secondhand.

chapters.title: Lag
chapters.summary: POV August. The delay grows to three seconds. August films the mirror and watches the footage: in the recording, her reflection turns its head while she stands still. She smashes the bathroom mirror; the shards each hold a tiny, intact reflection. Emotional beat: the skeptic's framework cracking under data she can't falsify.

chapters.title: Through the Glass, Backwards
chapters.summary: POV August. Investigating the bricked arch at 3 a.m., August sees light through the mortar — and her own reflection in the brick, waving when she doesn't. She touches it and falls through into the house as it was in 1974, warm, lit, and occupied. Emotional beat: vertigo and terrible wonder.

chapters.title: Summer, 1974
chapters.summary: POV August. She navigates the living past carefully, finding her grandmother young, laughing, alive — and a second little girl in family photos no one acknowledges. The house smells of lake water no one else notices. Emotional beat: longing for a family she never had, shadowed by wrongness.

chapters.title: The Girl in the Lake House
chapters.summary: POV August. August learns the unacknowledged girl is Denny Marsh, a neighbor's daughter who drowned in July 1974 — or didn't, because here Denny is still visiting, still dripping, still smiling too widely. Adults flinch when Denny enters a room. Emotional beat: pity sharpening into alarm.

chapters.title: It Wears Her Well
chapters.summary: POV August. August witnesses 'Denny' alone: its smile holds when the rest of its face goes slack, and mirrors refuse it entirely. It speaks to August in her own voice, offering to trade — 'a face for a face, a summer for a summer.' Emotional beat: recognition of the predator behind the child.

chapters.title: Tally Marks
chapters.summary: POV August. Counting the scratches on the arch (now visible in both times), August realizes they count days, not victims — someone survived down there for over a year. She finds initials: E.C., her grandmother's. Emotional beat: horrified respect; her grandmother fought this thing and won, somehow.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Ruth (1974 interlude). Ruth recounts, in the present day via a recorded tape August finds, how Edith Crane hid in the tunnels with Denny's photograph — the anchor binding the Smile to this place — and how Edith paid for her survival with the memory of that entire summer. Emotional beat: guilt passed down like an heirloom.

chapters.title: The Photograph
chapters.summary: POV August. Following the tape's clues, August locates the hiding place in the wall cavity: a tin containing Denny Marsh's last photograph, taken minutes before she drowned. The Smile appears behind her in the tunnel, patient, smiling. Emotional beat: triumph immediately outweighed by being cornered.

chapters.title: A Face for a Face
chapters.summary: POV August. Trapped in 1974, August bargains. The Smile explains its terms plainly: return the photograph and Denny rests, but someone must stay as keeper. It shows August her grandmother's stored memories like postcards. Emotional beat: moral vertigo — survival has always had a price here.

chapters.title: What Edith Forgot
chapters.summary: POV August. Among the stored memories August watches her grandmother's final night in the tunnels: Edith chose to forget rather than become the keeper, leaving the debt unpaid for fifty years. August understands the inheritance — the house, the lag, the pull. Emotional beat: anger at her grandmother dissolving into grief.

chapters.title: Sixty Seconds
chapters.summary: POV August. Back in the present, the mirror lag hits a full minute; reflections now act independently, mouthing warnings. August's own reflection begs her — in her voice — not to go back down. Emotional beat: isolation; even her mirrored self has become a separate frightened person.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Room
chapters.summary: POV August. August explores deeper than her grandmother ever dared and finds the keeper's room: a small dry chamber with a cot, tally marks, and the desiccated remains of the previous keeper — Denny's father, who went looking for his daughter in 1974 and never left. Emotional beat: the cost made flesh.

chapters.title: Bargaining with a Smile
chapters.summary: POV August. August offers a third option: not a face, not a life, but a memory — the Smile feeds on identity, so let it feed on hers by choice, once, fully, and release both Cranes. The Smile considers. It has never been offered anything willingly. Emotional beat: terrified courage.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV August. At the drowned hour of Denny's death, August returns the photograph to the lake's edge inside the tunnel as water floods the passage. Denny's true shape surfaces, thanks her, and comes apart like breath on glass. The Smile screams without opening its mouth. Emotional beat: catharsis amid catastrophe.

chapters.title: The Price Named Aloud
chapters.summary: POV August. The Smile accepts the bargain but takes more than agreed — it strips August's worst memory along with everything tying her to that summer, including why she descended. She crawls out of the collapsing tunnel into the present-day basement as the arch seals itself behind her. Emotional beat: survival and loss indistinguishable.

chapters.title: Edith
chapters.summary: POV August. In the emptied house, August finds her grandmother's presence waiting — freed by Denny's release — and they share one wordless hour before Edith fades. Neither remembers the tunnels, only that they are finished with them. Emotional beat: reconciliation without recollection; love outlasting memory.

chapters.title: Sold
chapters.summary: POV August. Weeks later, August sells the house to a developer who razes it; the survey crew finds no tunnels, no arch, no bones. August feels only a strange relief she can't source, and keeps a child's shoe on her shelf without knowing why. Emotional beat: uneasy peace, the wound that forgot itself.

chapters.title: The New Tenant Checks the Mirror
chapters.summary: POV Mara, the house's new owner, in an epilogue set before demolition. Unpacking in the empty house, Mara's cat stares at the bathroom mirror; Mara glances up and could swear the reflection smiled a half-second early. She laughs it off. Somewhere below, faintly, something begins counting again. Emotional beat: the cycle's quiet, chilling restart.
